segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Agrippa said to Paul,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are permitted to speak for yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Concerning everything I am accused of by Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself blessed that it is before you I am to make my defense today,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: especially since you are an expert in all the customs and controversies of the Jews. So I beg you to hear me patiently.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known to all Jews.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: They have known me from far back, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee, according to the strictest party of our religion.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And now I stand here being judged for hope in the promise God made to our fathers,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: the promise our twelve tribes hope to attain as they earnestly worship night and day. It is about this hope, O king, that I am accused by Jews!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Why is it judged unbelievable among you that God raises the dead?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things against the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And that is what I did in Jerusalem. I locked up many of the holy ones in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were being put to death I cast my vote against them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In all the synagogues I often punished them and tried to force them to blaspheme, and, raging madly against them beyond all measure, I persecuted them even as far as foreign cities.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In the course of this I was traveling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: when at midday on the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those traveling with me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But get up and stand on your feet. For this is why I have appeared to you: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of what you have seen of me and of the things in which I will appear to you,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I am sending you

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: to open their eyes, so that they turn from darkness to light and from the authority of Satan to God, and so that they receive forgiveness of sins and a share among those made holy by faith in me.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: but first to those in Damascus and in Jerusalem, and throughout the whole region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I declared that they should turn back and turn to God, doing deeds worthy of that turning back.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So, having received help from God, I stand to this day testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said was going to happen:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: that the Messiah was to suffer, and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he was to proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are mad, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am not mad, most excellent Festus. I am uttering words of truth and sound sense.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak freely; for I am not persuaded that any of this escapes him, since this was not done in a corner.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Agrippa said to Paul,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In so short a time you are persuading me to play the Christian!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul replied,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Whether in a short time or a long one, I would pray to God that not only you but all who are listening to me today might become such as I am, apart from these chains.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those seated with them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after they had withdrawn they were saying to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is doing nothing that deserves death or chains.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Agrippa said to Festus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

notes.note: Most translations render the word here as 'fortunate' or 'happy', treating it as a courtesy in a speech's opening. It is the same word as in the Beatitudes, and this translation renders it 'blessed' throughout so the reader can see that. In this context the sense is close to 'fortunate'.

The Greek word here is the same one translated 'Gentiles' in verses 17, 20 and 23. In the singular it means a people or nation, here Paul's own Jewish people. In the plural it usually means the non-Jewish peoples.

The word means a school or party within a larger body, and was used neutrally of philosophical schools and of Jewish groups such as the Pharisees and Sadducees. 'Sect' now suggests a breakaway or fringe group, which is not implied here. Many translations still use 'sect'.

The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

notes.traditional: gave my voice against them / cast my vote against them
notes.note: Literally 'I brought down a pebble', from the practice of voting with pebbles. Whether this means Paul was a voting member of the Sanhedrin or is a figure of speech for his approval, as at Stephen's death, is disputed.

notes.phrase: tried to force them to blaspheme
notes.note: The Greek tense can describe a repeated action ('I kept forcing them') or an attempted one ('I tried to force them'). Most modern translations take it as an attempt, without implying that it succeeded. The blasphemy meant is presumably cursing or renouncing Jesus.

The Greek expression can refer to Hebrew or to Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Judea and Galilee. Many scholars think Aramaic is meant, and some translations say so, but this is not certain. The form of the name, 'Saoul', reflects the Semitic original.

A goad is a pointed stick for driving oxen; an animal that kicks back at it only hurts itself. The phrase was a well-known Greek proverb for futile resistance to a greater power, especially a divine one, and is found in writers such as Euripides. It is about the futility of resisting. The words themselves do not point to a troubled conscience.

The traditional rendering is 'repent', with 'repentance' for the related noun at the end of the verse. 'Repent' now centres on feeling sorry, whereas the word carries the prophets' call to return to God in mind and conduct. It is paired here with a second verb meaning simply 'turn'. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term.

The Greek word is the one usually rendered 'Christ'. Here it is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and the point in dispute is whether that figure was to suffer, so 'Messiah' is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels and Acts.

notes.traditional: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian
notes.note: Agrippa's reply is difficult in Greek. It can mean 'you are persuading me to act the Christian', by an idiom with a Septuagint parallel, or 'you are trying to persuade me, so as to make me a Christian'. The opening phrase can mean 'in a short time' or 'with little effort'; the older 'almost' is now generally rejected. His tone, whether ironic, evasive or serious, is not marked, and Paul's answer picks up the same phrase.

candidates.reason: Recurs in Acts and the letters where translations vary between 'sect', 'party', 'faction' and 'heresy', and the variation changes how readers hear the early movement described.
Rendered 'serve' or 'worship' inconsistently across Luke-Acts, Paul, Hebrews and Revelation, and needs to be kept distinct from προσκυνέω and δουλεύω.
Occurs across the Gospels and Acts alongside Ναζαρηνός; a single decision is needed on 'of Nazareth', 'the Nazarene' or 'Nazorean'.
With μετανοέω fixed as 'turn back', the rendering of this frequent verb needs fixing so the two stay distinct where they are paired, as in Acts 3:19 and 26:20.
Translations waver between 'authority', 'power' and 'right' across the whole New Testament, hiding links such as that between delegated authority and Satan's dominion in this chapter.
